BUSS1020 Week 06

BUSS1020 Week 06 - Sampling Distributions: Sample Means, Sample Proportions, the Central Limit Theorem and the Finite Population Correction

Overview

This week explains how sample statistics behave, which is the bridge from describing data to making inferences:

• Estimating a population parameter with a sample statistic, and why different samples give different answers (sampling variation).

• The sampling distribution of the sample mean: unbiasedness, variance and standard error.

• The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): when the sample mean is approximately normal even if the population is not.

• The sampling distribution of the sample proportion p, and the conditions for using a normal approximation.

• The finite population correction (FPC) for sampling without replacement from a small population.

Key Concepts

Parameters, statistics and sampling variation

• The goal is usually a population parameter such as the population mean mu, but the population cannot be fully observed. Instead a sample x1, ..., xn is drawn and the statistic x-bar = sum of xi / n is computed, because sampling is cheaper and faster than a census.

• Sampling variation: even with correct random sampling, different samples produce different values of x-bar. This variation is not a mistake; it is an inherent feature of taking samples.

• A sampling distribution describes a statistic as a random variable: which values it can take, and how likely each value is across all possible samples of the same size.

The sampling distribution of the sample mean

Unless a finite-population correction is stated, observations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed random draws. Here n is sample size, mu is the population mean, sigma is the population standard deviation, and sigma squared is its variance.

• Expected value: E(X-bar) = mu. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean: the centre of its sampling distribution is exactly mu. A single sample might give 19 or 23, but on average the procedure is correct.

• Variance: Var(X-bar) = sigma squared / n. Standard deviation of the sample mean, called the standard error: SE(X-bar) = sigma / square root of n.

• The name "standard error" marks it as the error introduced by sampling: it measures how much x-bar fluctuates from sample to sample. It is not the standard deviation of the individual observations.

• Effect of sample size: SE(4n) = sigma / (2 square root of n) = half of SE(n). Multiplying the sample size by 4 cuts the standard error in half; cutting it further requires much larger samples.

• If the population itself is normal, then X-bar is exactly normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma / square root of n, for any sample size. This is an exact result, not an approximation.

• For a normal sampling distribution, about 95% of all sample means lie in the interval mu plus or minus 1.96 sigma / square root of n.

The Central Limit Theorem

• The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that for a sufficiently large sample size, the sample mean X-bar is approximately normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma / square root of n, no matter what shape the population distribution has. For the usual version, the observations must be independent and identically distributed, with a finite mean and a finite, non-zero standard deviation.

• Practical rules of thumb: n greater than 30 works for most population shapes; if the population is fairly symmetric, about n = 15 can be enough.

• Mechanism: averaging lets large and small observations cancel. Starting from a uniform or an exponential population, the sampling distributions for n = 2, 5, 30 become progressively more bell-shaped.

• Why it matters: it allows probabilities for X-bar to be computed with the normal distribution even when the population shape is unknown or strange, so sampling error can be quantified without enumerating the whole population.

• Scope: the CLT describes the sampling distribution of a statistic. It does not make individual observations, or individual errors, normally distributed.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion

• Notation: pi is the population proportion (a parameter), p is the sample proportion (a statistic). If X ~ Binomial(n, pi), then p = X / n.

• Expected value: E(p) = pi, so the sample proportion is unbiased.

• Variance and standard deviation: Var(p) = pi(1 - pi)/n, so SD(p) = sqrt[pi(1 - pi)/n].

• Standardized form: Z = (p - pi) / sqrt[pi(1 - pi)/n].

• Normal-approximation condition for proportions: n pi >= 5 AND n(1 - pi) >= 5, both at the same time. The sample must be large enough and the population must contain enough members with (and without) the attribute. Even a huge n fails the condition if the attribute is very rare.

• The exact distribution of p = X/n is the binomial distribution rescaled: its possible values are 0, 1/n, 2/n, ..., 1. Before a normal approximation is applied, p is not free to take any number between 0 and 1.

The finite population correction

When sampling is without replacement from a finite population and the sample is large relative to the population (n/N greater than 0.05), the standard error must be adjusted with the finite population correction:

• FPC = square root of (N - n)/(N - 1).

• Adjusted standard error of the mean: sigma_x-bar = (sigma / square root of n) x FPC.

• Adjusted standard deviation of the proportion: sigma_p = sqrt[pi(1 - pi)/n] x FPC.

Five points:

The FPC is less than 1 (for n greater than 1), so it always reduces the standard error: removing units as they are sampled leaves relatively more information in each observation. For n = 1 the factor equals 1 and there is nothing to correct.

Sampling with replacement needs no correction, because drawn units return to the pool and every draw is independent.

In practice, when the sample exceeds about 5% of the population, both the sample mean and the sample proportion get the corrected standard error.

The same factor multiplies the hypergeometric standard deviation, because both describe sampling without replacement from a finite population.

If the population size N is not given, treat the population as effectively infinite and apply no correction.

Standard errors in Excel

• Probabilities about a sample mean use the standard error sigma / square root of n, not the population standard deviation itself.

• STDEV.P(data)/SQRT(n) is only valid when the data are the entire population in question. When the standard deviation is estimated from a sample, use STDEV.S(sample)/SQRT(n).

• The standard error is compared with the population standard deviation to show how much averaging reduces variation; comparing it with the population mean would be meaningless.

Worked Examples

The same structure in three business settings

• A taste test surveys 50 people to estimate the share who like a new drink: the statistic is the sample proportion p.

• A retailer surveys 25 customers to estimate average annual spending: the statistic is the sample mean x-bar.

• A cereal manufacturer weighs boxes coming off the line to check the average fill: again the sample mean x-bar.

Each case uses one sample statistic to say something about a population parameter, and each answer varies from sample to sample.

A complete sampling experiment: population of four values

A small population has four values: 18, 20, 22, 24 (for example the number of business meetings held per month).

Population mean: mu = (18 + 20 + 22 + 24)/4 = 84/4 = 21.

Population variance: sigma squared = [(18-21)² + (20-21)² + (22-21)² + (24-21)²]/4 = (9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5, so sigma = square root of 5 = 2.236.

Draw all samples of size n = 2 with replacement: 4 x 4 = 16 possible samples.

Unbiasedness: E(X-bar) = (18x1 + 19x2 + 20x3 + 21x4 + 22x3 + 23x2 + 24x1)/16 = 336/16 = 21 = mu.

Reduced spread: Var(X-bar) = sum of (x-bar - 21)² x frequency / 16 = 40/16 = 2.5, so SD(X-bar) = square root of 2.5 = 1.58, well below the population standard deviation of 2.236. Averaging lets large and small values cancel.

Related point: taking a sample equal to the population size (n = N) removes sampling variation only when the sampling is without replacement, that is a census. With replacement, even n = N leaves variation in x-bar, as the table shows.

Where do 95% of sample means fall?

A normal population has mu = 368, sigma = 15, and samples of n = 25 are drawn.

Standard error: SE = 15 / square root of 25 = 3.

The 95% range: mu plus or minus 1.96 SE = 368 plus or minus 1.96(3) = 368 plus or minus 5.88 = [362.12, 373.88].

Interpretation: if sampling is repeated many times with n = 25, about 95% of the sample means land in this interval. If a machine is genuinely filling to 500 grams, 95% of sample means must fall in a computable band around 500; a sample mean outside that band is a signal that something has changed. This logic is the foundation of confidence intervals.

CLT in action: probability for a sample mean

A population has mu = 8 and sigma = 3 (its shape is unknown). For n = 36, find P(7.8 < X-bar < 8.2).

Standard error: SE = 3 / square root of 36 = 0.5.

Standardize both bounds: z_low = (7.8 - 8)/0.5 = -0.4; z_high = (8.2 - 8)/0.5 = 0.4.

P is approximately Phi(0.4) - Phi(-0.4) = 0.6554 - 0.3446 = 0.3108, about 31%.

Phi denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function. With independent random draws, n = 36 supports the usual normal approximation for many population shapes, but 30 is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee for extremely skewed or heavy-tailed populations.

CLT in quality control: is the machine overfilling?

A cereal manufacturer targets 500 grams per box, with a process standard deviation of 20 grams. A sample of n = 50 boxes has mean x-bar = 510 grams. If the true mean really is 500, how likely is a sample mean of 510 or more?

Standard error: SE = 20 / square root of 50 = 2.8284.

z = (510 - 500)/2.8284 = 3.5355.

P(X-bar >= 510) = P(Z >= 3.5355) = 0.000203, about 0.02%.

Decision: about 99.7% of a standard normal lies between -3 and 3, and 3.54 is well outside. Under the stated model, a probability of about two in ten thousand is strong evidence against a mean of 500 grams in the direction of overfilling. Sampling variation remains possible; calibration, sampling and process assumptions should be investigated.

Sampling proportions in a poll

In a poll about a tax change, the true support proportion is pi = 0.40 and n = 200 people are surveyed. What is the probability that the sample proportion lands between 0.40 and 0.45?

Standard deviation of p: SD(p) = square root of 0.4 x 0.6 / 200 = square root of 0.0012 = 0.03464.

z for 0.40 is 0; z for 0.45 is (0.45 - 0.40)/0.03464 = 1.4434.

P(0.40 <= p <= 0.45) = Phi(1.4434) - Phi(0) = 0.9255 - 0.5 = 0.4255, about 42.5% (rounding z to 1.44 gives 0.4251).

By symmetry, P(0.35 <= p <= 0.45) is about twice that, roughly 85%. Here plus or minus 5 percentage points gives roughly 85% normal-approximation coverage, not the conventional 95%. A 95% margin under this model is about 1.96 x 0.03464 = 0.0679, or 6.8 percentage points.

Sampling proportions in a product decision

A new drink is profitable only if at least 10% of customers buy it. In a sample of n = 50, only 4 people, that is 8%, say they would buy. Does this prove the product will fail?

Assume the true proportion is pi = 0.10. Then SD(p) = square root of 0.10 x 0.90 / 50 = square root of 0.0018 = 0.042426.

z = (0.08 - 0.10)/0.042426 = -0.4714.

The uncorrected normal approximation gives Phi(-0.4714), about 0.32. Because n pi = 5 is borderline and p is discrete, the exact binomial probability is preferable: P(X <= 4) = sum from k = 0 to 4 of C(50,k)(0.1)^k(0.9)^(50-k), about 0.4312.

Decision: if the true share really were 10%, a sample result of 8% or lower would happen about 43% of the time under the exact binomial model. That is ordinary sampling variation, so 8% is not evidence that the product will fail.

Contrast with the quality-control example: whether an observed number is surprising can only be judged by comparing it with the sampling distribution of the statistic, never by intuition alone. A 2% shift was decisive there (probability 0.02%); a 2% shift here is unremarkable (exact probability about 43%).

Finite population correction in practice

A sample of n = 100 is drawn without replacement from a population of N = 1000. The sample mean is x-bar = 9 and the standard deviation is 40.

Sample fraction: n/N = 100/1000 = 10% > 5%, so the FPC applies.

Uncorrected standard error: SE = 40 / square root of 100 = 4.

FPC = square root of (1000 - 100)/(1000 - 1) = square root of 900/999 = 0.9492.

Corrected standard error: 4 x 0.9492 = 3.80.

95% interval for the mean: 9 plus or minus 1.96(3.80) = 9 plus or minus 7.45 = [1.55, 16.45].

The procedure to remember: divide sigma by square root of n first, then multiply by the FPC.
